article_title: Affordances and Challenges of Incorporating a Remote, Cloud-accessible Quantum Experiment into Undergraduate Courses
citation: Victoria Borish and H. J. Lewandowski. (2025). Affordances and Challenges of Incorporating a Remote, Cloud-accessible Quantum Experiment into Undergraduate Courses. arXiv:2502.00613. https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.00613
title: Oqtant: a publicly available cloud-accessible Bose-Einstein condensate experiment for education
description: Oqtant is a remote ultracold-atom experiment hosted by Infleqtion that users control over the internet via a web application or Python API, submitting jobs that create and manipulate BECs and receiving images and basic analysis back. The article states it is "the only publicly-available quantum experiment hosted by a quantum company that is not a quantum computer of which we are aware." Users adjust evaporative cooling parameters, apply a repulsive laser to manipulate the condensate, and obtain atomic density profiles from which atom number and temperature are calculated.
requirements: An internet connection and a free account; jobs run only when the experiment is online, with free accounts limited to between 10 and 20 jobs per day and a maximum of 100 jobs per month
constraints: The experiment was online only limited hours (10 am to 3 pm Mountain time Tuesdays through Thursdays every other week in its first year), and in September 2024 Infleqtion announced an indefinite pause of services beginning November 2024
target_learning_goals: experimental skills with quantum matter platforms
understanding Bose-Einstein condensates and quantum phenomena such as superposition, interference, and tunneling
examples: Users submit jobs containing experimental parameters, and once a job completes they access the resulting image of the atoms along with Oqtant's calculated atom number and temperature
key_sources: Victoria Borish and H. J. Lewandowski. (2025). Affordances and Challenges of Incorporating a Remote, Cloud-accessible Quantum Experiment into Undergraduate Courses. arXiv:2502.00613. https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.00613

citation: Victoria Borish and H. J. Lewandowski. (2025). Affordances and Challenges of Incorporating a Remote, Cloud-accessible Quantum Experiment into Undergraduate Courses. arXiv:2502.00613. https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.00613
title: Two structured Jupyter-notebook activities on ultracold atoms and BEC creation designed for upper-division courses
description: The authors developed a sequence of two activities, each taking students two to three hours plus roughly half an hour of preparation, structured as Jupyter notebooks in which students submit runs to Oqtant, analyze returned data, and answer reflection questions. The article reports that "Each of the activities and preparation activities included explicit learning goals, so the students would know what they were expected to learn from the activities." Activity 1 covers absorption imaging and extracting atom number and temperature; Activity 2 covers BEC creation, bimodal fits, critical temperature, and aspect-ratio comparisons.
requirements: Students need basic Python programming knowledge including generating basic plotting commands, using for loops, and slightly adjusting already-written code
constraints: The activities were designed assuming minimal student prior knowledge of BECs but were somewhat structured due to the complexity of Oqtant
target_learners: upper-division undergraduate physics students in quantum mechanics or beyond-first-year lab courses
target_learning_goals: understanding BEC formation and quantum behavior
examples: In the first activity students analyze already-taken Oqtant data using 2D Gaussian fits, then submit their own runs choosing requested temperatures; in the second they compare Gaussian and bimodal fits and find the critical temperature
